common_name: Victoria Red Grape (Pierce's Disease-Tolerant Table Grape)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container-grown vines in spring in full sun in well-drained soil; Victoria Red is a jointly released University of Arkansas / Texas A&M AgriLife table grape named a 2017 Texas Superstar for its sustained tolerance to Pierce's disease, the bacterial disease that kills most table and wine grapes throughout the humid Gulf South within a few years.

directions: Train on a trellis system in full sun in well-drained soil; prune in late winter. Victoria Red is a seeded red table grape that has survived over 25 years of extreme Pierce's disease pressure at the Tarkington Vineyards test site near Victoria, Texas, making it one of the few table grapes with genuinely sustained tolerance to the disease that otherwise makes grape growing across the Gulf Coast so difficult. It produces large, sweet clusters with sugar levels reaching up to 25 brix, eaten fresh, dried into raisins, or made into juice. Because it was bred specifically for hot, humid Texas and Gulf Coast conditions, it needs none of the intensive spray programs required to keep Pierce's-disease-susceptible European grapes alive in the region. Harvest clusters once berries have colored fully and taste sweet, since grapes do not continue ripening after picking.
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Pierce's Disease-Tolerant Grapes
University of Arkansas System Division of Agriculture

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container-grown vines in spring in full sun in well-drained soil; Roucaneuf is a French-American hybrid grape (Seyve-Villard lineage) documented by Texas A&M AgriLife Extension as resistant to Pierce's disease and well suited to hot, dry Gulf South and Texas conditions.

directions: Train on a cordon trellis system in full sun in well-drained soil; prune in late winter. Roucaneuf is a complex French-American hybrid grape carrying genes from several wild American Vitis species alongside European vinifera, giving it real resistance to Pierce's disease, the bacterial infection spread by sharpshooter insects that kills most European wine grapes across the humid Gulf South within a few seasons. It is one of a small group of Pierce's-disease-resistant varieties recommended by Texas A&M AgriLife Extension for gardeners and small growers in the region who want to make wine or juice without the constant disease losses that come with standard vinifera grapes. Harvest clusters once berries have colored and developed good sugar content, and expect the vigorous vines to need regular summer pruning to manage growth in a warm, humid climate.
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Pierce's Disease-Tolerant Grapes

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun; Freedom is a Cornell-Geneva breeding program release that is field-immune to apple scab and highly resistant to cedar apple rust and powdery mildew, needing little or no fungicide spraying.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator. Freedom was released by Cornell University's Geneva breeding program and is field-immune to apple scab, one of the most damaging fungal diseases of apple in humid climates, while also showing high resistance to cedar apple rust and powdery mildew. The medium-large, red-striped fruit is crisp and juicy with a tart, tangy flavor good for fresh eating and cooking, and it stores reasonably well for a few months under cool conditions. Because it needs so little disease-management spraying, Freedom is a strong choice for a low-input or organic home orchard. Plant with a compatible pollinator variety for good fruit set, and harvest once fruit has developed full color and comes away easily from the spur with a gentle twist.
sources: Purdue Cooperative Extension — Apple Disease Resistance Ratings

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun; Redfree is a Purdue-Rutgers-Illinois (PRI) breeding program release, field-immune to apple scab and resistant to the other major apple diseases, and ripens earlier than most disease-resistant apples.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator. Redfree was released by the Purdue-Rutgers-Illinois cooperative breeding program in 1981 and is field-immune to apple scab while also resisting the other major fungal and bacterial apple diseases, making it one of the most reliably low-spray apples available. It ripens earlier than most disease-resistant varieties, giving a mid-to-late-summer crop of medium-sized, bright red, crisp, juicy fruit with a mild, sweet flavor good for fresh eating. Because it is one of the earliest scab-immune apples to ripen, Redfree is a good choice for gardeners who want disease resistance without waiting until fall for the harvest. Plant with a compatible pollinator variety and pick fruit once it has developed full color and separates easily from the spur.
sources: Purdue Cooperative Extension — Apple Disease Resistance Ratings

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun; Priscilla was one of the earliest releases from the Purdue-Rutgers-Illinois disease-resistance breeding program, rated very resistant to apple scab and also resistant to fire blight and cedar apple rust.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator. Priscilla was introduced in 1972 by the Purdue-Rutgers-Illinois cooperative breeding program and rates very resistant to apple scab while also resisting fire blight and cedar apple rust, letting a home orchard get by with little or no fungicide spraying. The medium-sized, red-striped fruit has crisp, juicy, mildly tart flesh good for fresh eating and cooking, ripening in late summer to early fall. As one of the earlier disease-resistant apple releases, Priscilla helped establish the case that good disease resistance and good eating quality did not have to be a trade-off. Plant with a compatible pollinator variety and harvest once fruit has developed full color and separates easily from the spur with a gentle twist.
sources: Purdue Cooperative Extension — Apple Disease Resistance Ratings

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun; Jonafree is a Purdue-Rutgers-Illinois (PRI) breeding program release bred to bring classic Jonathan flavor into a scab-resistant, low-spray apple, also resisting powdery mildew, fire blight, and cedar apple rust.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator. Jonafree was bred by the Purdue-Rutgers-Illinois cooperative program to capture the classic tangy-sweet flavor of the old Jonathan apple in a tree resistant to apple scab, powdery mildew, fire blight, and cedar apple rust, sparing home growers the heavy fungicide schedule that susceptible heirloom apples like Jonathan itself require. The medium-sized, bright red fruit has crisp, juicy flesh with the familiar sprightly Jonathan flavor, good for fresh eating, sauce, and baking. Because it combines classic flavor with broad disease resistance, Jonafree is a good choice for gardeners who love old-fashioned apple flavor but want a low-spray, low-maintenance tree. Plant with a compatible pollinator variety and harvest once fruit has developed full color and separates easily from the spur.
sources: Purdue Cooperative Extension — Apple Disease Resistance Ratings

common_name: Southern Bartlett Pear (Low-Chill Gulf Coast Bartlett Sport)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in well-drained, fertile loam in full sun; plant with a second pear cultivar (such as Warren, Hood, or Kieffer) for cross-pollination. Southern Bartlett is a chance sport of Bartlett found on an old Louisiana homestead, selected for its low chilling requirement of roughly 350-400 hours, letting it fruit reliably in Gulf Coast winters too mild for standard Bartlett.

directions: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in well-drained, fertile loam in full sun; Southern Bartlett is a chance sport of the classic Bartlett pear discovered on an old Louisiana homestead and selected specifically for its low chilling requirement, letting it set fruit reliably in the mild Gulf Coast winters that leave standard Bartlett trees short on the cold hours they need to flower well. It bears the same classic bell-shaped, buttery, sweet pear fruit familiar from Bartlett, ripening in mid to late summer. Like most European pears grown in the humid South, it remains more vulnerable to fire blight along the immediate Gulf Coast than truly blight-resistant Southern selections such as Warren or Ayers, so prune out and destroy any blighted shoots promptly and avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer, which encourages the soft new growth blight favors. Harvest while still firm and green-yellow, then ripen off the tree at room temperature for the best buttery texture and flavor.
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Fruit and Nut Resources
Harris County (Texas) Cooperative Extension — Fruit Variety Guide
